Ladies and gentlemen, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, entrepreneurs, and colleagues, it is a great honor to address you today at the United Nations MSME Day. Around the world, micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises face an increasingly complex reality. They operate in a world shaped by geopolitical uncertainty, climate-related disruptions, digital transformation, supply chain volatility, and social change. In this environment, one concept has become strategic imperative: resilience. Every government wants resilient economies, every community wants resilient businesses, and every entrepreneur wants a resilient organization that can survive and thrive in times of disruption. Yet resilience does not emerge by accident. The question is: What creates organizational resilience? Our research suggests that part of the answers lies in a concept known as human entrepreneurship. Human entrepreneurship is a human-centered approach to entrepreneurship and management. It combines entrepreneurial orientation with a deep commitment to people and sustainable value creation. At its core, there are four principles: empathy, equity, enablement, and empowerment. Together, these principles create organizational environments in which people are trusted, included, developed, encouraged to contribute their full potential. Why does this matter? Because resilience is ultimately a human capability. Organizations do not adapt, people do. Organizations do not innovate, people do. Organizations do not overcome crisis, people do. When employees feel valued, trusted, and empowered, they become more engaged, more innovative, and more willing to respond proactively to uncertainty and change. This is where the connection between human entrepreneurship, organizational sustainability, and organizational resilience become visible. Organizational sustainability is often understood as a long-term pursuit of economic prosperity, social well-being, and environmental responsibility. Organizational resilience in contrast, refers to a capability to anticipate disruption, adapt to changing conditions, and recover from adversity. Traditionally, this concept has been discussed separately. However, research has shown that they are deeply interconnected. Sustainability provides the direction, resilience provides the capability, and human entrepreneurship provides the human foundation that makes both possible. By investing in human and social capital, organizations strengthen their capability to innovate, learn, collaborate, and adapt. These capabilities enable them not only to withstand crisis but to pursue sustainable development over the long term. In other words, human-centered organizations become sustainable organizations. Sustainable organizations become, with resilient organizations, and resilient organizations create long-term value for society. For policymakers, this carries important implications. We should develop entrepreneurial ecosystems that promote collaboration, trust, and shared value creation.
